title: Sets: std::set and std::unordered_set
summary: Keep unique values with std::set, query them in order, combine sets, and know when to use unordered_set and multiset.
intro: A map stores a value for every key. Sometimes you only need the keys: which IDs visited, which tags exist, which skills match. A set stores each value once, keeps it sorted, and answers "is it here?" in O(log n).

steps.title: Unique, sorted values
steps.body:
A `std::set<T>` from `<set>` holds unique values and keeps them sorted. Inserting a value that is already there does nothing, so a set is the natural tool for removing duplicates.

```cpp
std::vector<int> v = {5, 1, 5, 3};
std::set<int> s(v.begin(), v.end());  // {1, 3, 5}
s.insert(3);                          // already there, ignored
s.size();                             // 3
s.count(5);                           // 1 if present, 0 if not
s.erase(1);                           // removes 1, returns how many it removed
```

The range constructor `s(v.begin(), v.end())` copies every element of the vector and drops the repeats. A range-for walks the set in ascending order, and strings come out alphabetically. A set has no index for the `if (i > 0)` separator trick, so keep a `bool first` flag instead. Like map insert, `s.insert(x)` returns `{iterator, bool}`, so `s.insert(x).second` tells you whether the value was new.

In memory a set is a map with keys only, built on the same sorted tree (a red-black tree in g++): every element lives in its own heap node with pointers to its parent and children. That makes insert, count, and erase O(log n), but a set uses more memory than a vector of the same values.

> Gotcha: set elements are const, because changing one in place would break the sorted order. To change a value, erase the old one and insert the new one.

example.title: Unique visitors
example.prompt: Count the unique visitor IDs, check one ID, remove another, and print the rest in order.
example.explanation: The range constructor turns six IDs into the set {3, 7, 19, 42}. Inserting 5 adds a fifth value, while inserting 42 again changes nothing, so `size()` is 5. `count(19)` is 1 because 19 is present. After `erase(7)` the range-for visits the IDs smallest first, and the `first` flag puts a space only between values.

practice.title: Blog tags
practice.prompt:
Collect the unique tags from a list of blog posts and print them alphabetically.

1. Build a `std::set<std::string>` named `tags` from `posts` with the range constructor.
2. Insert `"rust"` (new) and `"web"` (a duplicate).
3. Print the number of unique tags.
4. Use `count` to print `has cpp: ` followed by `true` or `false` (use `std::boolalpha`).
5. Erase `"games"`, then print the remaining tags on one line, separated by single spaces.

Expected output:

```text
5
has cpp: true
ai cpp rust web
```

tests.output:
5
has cpp: true
ai cpp rust web

hints: Pass `posts.begin()` and `posts.end()` to the set when you declare it, and it drops the repeated tags for you.
Inserting `"web"` again leaves the size unchanged. Print `(tags.count("cpp") == 1)` after `std::boolalpha`.
Iterate with `for (const auto& tag : tags)` and use a `bool first` flag to print a space before every tag except the first.

steps.title: Smallest, largest, and bounds
steps.body:
Because a set is sorted, its ends and its neighbors are cheap to reach.

```cpp
*s.begin();         // smallest element
*s.rbegin();        // largest element
s.find(x);          // iterator to x, or s.end()
s.lower_bound(x);   // first element >= x, or s.end()
s.upper_bound(x);   // first element > x, or s.end()
```

Every search returns an iterator, and `s.end()` means "no such element". Always compare with `end()` before you dereference, because `*s.end()` is undefined behavior. The if with an initializer keeps the iterator local:

```cpp
if (auto it = s.lower_bound(10); it != s.end()) {
    std::cout << *it << '\n';
}
```

The same rule applies to the ends: `*s.begin()` on an empty set is undefined behavior, so check `!s.empty()` first when the set might be empty.

`lower_bound` and `upper_bound` differ only when `x` itself is in the set: lower_bound stops on it, upper_bound skips past it.

> Gotcha: call the member `s.lower_bound(x)`, which walks the tree in O(log n). The free `std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x)` also compiles, but set iterators can only step one node at a time, so it takes O(n) steps.

example.title: Free seats
example.prompt: Answer questions about a set of free seat numbers: the ends, one membership check, and the next free seat from a few starting points.
example.explanation: `begin()` points at the smallest seat and `rbegin()` at the largest. `find(8)` returns an iterator to 8, which is not `end()`, so the comparison prints `true`. No seat is 16, so `lower_bound(16)` lands on the next one, 21. `upper_bound(15)` skips the 15 itself and also lands on 21. Nothing is at or after 31, so `lower_bound(31)` returns `end()` and the else branch prints `none`.

practice.title: Meeting starts
practice.prompt:
Answer questions about a set of meeting start hours.

1. Print the earliest and latest start on one line, separated by a space.
2. Use `find` to print whether a meeting starts at 11, as `true` or `false`.
3. Print the first start at or after 13 with `lower_bound`.
4. Print the first start after 13 with `upper_bound`.
5. Print the first start at or after 17 with `lower_bound`, or `none` when there is none.

Check every search result against `starts.end()` before you dereference it, and print `none` when it is `end()`.

Expected output:

```text
9 16
true
13
16
none
```
hints: `*starts.begin()` is the earliest and `*starts.rbegin()` the latest.
13 is in the set, so `lower_bound(13)` stops on it while `upper_bound(13)` moves on to 16.
Keep each search in an if with initializer, compare the iterator with `starts.end()`, and print `none` in the else branch.

steps.title: Union, intersection, difference
steps.body:
`<algorithm>` has three functions that combine two sorted ranges in one linear pass:

- `std::set_intersection`: values in both
- `std::set_union`: values in either
- `std::set_difference`: values in the first but not the second

Each takes two ranges and an output iterator. To write into a set, use `std::inserter` from `<iterator>`, which calls `insert` for every value it receives:

```cpp
std::set<int> both;
std::set_intersection(a.begin(), a.end(), b.begin(), b.end(),
                      std::inserter(both, both.begin()));
```

A plain `both.begin()` does not work. An iterator only points at elements that already exist and cannot add new ones. `std::inserter` turns each write into an insert.

Order matters for the difference: `a` minus `b` keeps what only `a` has, and swapping the ranges gives what only `b` has.

> Gotcha: the inputs must be sorted. A set always is, so sets just work. If you start from vectors, `std::sort` them first, or the result is silently wrong.

example.title: Class rosters
example.prompt: Compare the students in Math and Art: who takes both, who takes either, and who takes only Math.
example.output:
both: ben cy
either: ana ben cy dee
only math: ana
example.explanation: Both rosters are sets, so they are already sorted, which the three algorithms require. Each call reads the two ranges once and hands every matching name to `std::inserter`, which inserts it into the result set. `set_difference(math, art)` keeps only `ana`, the one name that Math has and Art does not. `printLine` prints a space before each name, so there is no trailing space.

practice.title: Skill match
practice.prompt:
Compare the skills a job requires with the skills a candidate has.

1. Put the skills in both sets into `matched` with `std::set_intersection`.
2. Put the required skills the candidate lacks into `missing` with `std::set_difference`.
3. Put every skill from either set into `combined` with `std::set_union`.
4. Write each result with `std::inserter`, then print the three sets with `printLine` using the labels `matched`, `missing`, and `all`.

Expected output:

```text
matched: git sql
missing: cpp linux
all: cpp git linux python sql
```

tests.output:
matched: git sql
missing: cpp linux
all: cpp git linux python sql

hints: Each call takes `required.begin(), required.end(), candidate.begin(), candidate.end()` and then `std::inserter(result, result.begin())`.
For `missing`, pass `required` first: the difference keeps what the first range has and the second does not.

steps.title: unordered_set and multiset
steps.body:
`std::unordered_set` from `<unordered_set>` is a hash set. It has the same `insert`, `count`, `find`, and `erase`, but they run in O(1) on average instead of O(log n) (O(n) in the rare worst case when many values share a bucket). The price: there is no order, so no `lower_bound`, no smallest or largest, no set algorithms from step 3, and iteration order is unspecified. Use it for fast membership checks and never print it in iteration order.

`std::multiset` (also in `<set>`) is a sorted set that keeps duplicates. `ms.count(x)` tells you how many copies there are. Erasing needs care:

```cpp
ms.erase(x);                   // removes EVERY copy of x
if (auto it = ms.find(x); it != ms.end()) {
    ms.erase(it);              // removes exactly one copy
}
```

> Gotcha: always check `find` before erasing through it. When `x` is missing, `find` returns `end()`, and `ms.erase(ms.end())` is undefined behavior.

In memory an unordered_set keeps a heap array of buckets, and each element sits in a node in the bucket its hash picks. As it grows it rehashes into a bigger bucket array, which is another reason its iteration order is not something to rely on.

example.title: Repeats and scores
example.prompt: Find the first repeated number with an unordered_set, then remove one and then all copies of a score from a multiset.
example.explanation: The loop checks each number against `seen` before adding it. 4, 9, and 2 are new, and the second 9 is the first one already present, so the loop prints it and stops. The order of `seen` never matters because it is never printed. The multiset keeps all three 90s in sorted order. Erasing through the checked `find` removes one copy, and `erase(90)` then removes the remaining two.

practice.title: Repeats and ages
practice.prompt:
Find the first repeated word, then remove copies of an age from a multiset.

1. Walk `words` with a `std::unordered_set<std::string>` named `seen` and print `first repeat: ` followed by the first word that is already in `seen`, then stop.
2. Build a `std::multiset<int>` holding 30, 25, 30, 41, 30 and print `count(30)`.
3. Erase a single 30 through `find`, after checking the result against `end()`, and print the ages with `printAges`.
4. Remove the remaining 30s with `erase(30)` and print the ages again.

Expected output:

```text
first repeat: blue
3
25 30 30 41
25 41
```
hints: Check `seen.count(word) == 1` before inserting the word, and `break` as soon as it is true.
Erasing the iterator that `find` returns removes just one copy. Compare it with `ages.end()` first.
`ages.erase(30)` with a value removes every remaining copy.

recap:
- `std::set<T>` from `<set>` stores unique values in ascending order. `insert` ignores duplicates, `count` checks membership, and `erase` removes a value.
- `std::set<int> s(v.begin(), v.end())` builds a set from a vector and drops the repeats.
- A set is a sorted tree of heap nodes, like a map without values: O(log n) operations, and elements are const, so change one by erasing and inserting.
- `*s.begin()` is the smallest and `*s.rbegin()` the largest, on a non-empty set.
- `find`, `lower_bound` (first >= x), and `upper_bound` (first > x) return `end()` when nothing matches, so check before dereferencing.
- Use the member `s.lower_bound(x)` (O(log n)), not `std::lower_bound` on a set (O(n)).
- `std::set_union`, `std::set_intersection`, and `std::set_difference` need sorted inputs and write through `std::inserter(result, result.begin())` from `<iterator>`.
- `std::unordered_set` is a hash set: O(1) average, no order, so never print it in iteration order.
- `std::multiset` keeps duplicates sorted. `erase(x)` removes every copy, `erase(s.find(x))` removes one after you check `find` against `end()`.
